newsitem.title: INDIA: India plans bonds to wipe out $4.3 bln oil deficit.
newsitem.headline: India plans bonds to wipe out $4.3 bln oil deficit.

text.p: The Indian government plans to pay off 155 billion rupees ($4.34 billion) it owes to state-run oil companies through the issue of 10-year bonds, a senior Petroleum Ministry official said on Monday.

The debt was accumulated during 1996/97 (March-April) because oil companies sold crude and products below market prices to support India's complex cross-subsidy system known as the administered pricing mechanism.
State-run oil companies are facing a severe liquidity crunch because of the government's delay in repaying them.
"A meeting of senior officers will be held today to decide the terms of trading these bonds and its yield rate," the official, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters.
Issuing bonds would effectively put the so-called "oil pool deficit" on the government's fiscal deficit.

While the Finance Ministry wants a lock-in period on these bonds, the Petroleum Ministry is recommending the companies be allowed to sell the bonds immediately to raise much needed cash, the official said.
Finance Ministry officials said last week they were concerned about consequent expansionary effects on money supply if the companies were allowed to sell the bonds immediately.
India's coalition government is facing opposition from leftist partners to a planned rise in petroleum product prices, which is one option to whittle down the oil pool deficit.
Oil companies have been urging the government to pay back the money they are owed, saying further delays could seriously hamper their ability to pay for refinery feedstock and long-term investment.
Officials are struggling to find an option that would limit the size of any needed fuel price rises.
Monday's meeting hopes to resolve the difference between the two ministries over the rate of interest payable on such bonds, the official said.
At a previous meeting, Finance Ministry officials suggested that the annual interest rate on the bonds be less than 10 percent, but the Petroleum Ministry wants the rate fixed at 10.5 percent.

The panel of top civil servants of the departments of petroleum, revenue, expenditure and the Planning Commission will also deliberate on Monday ways to bridge the deficit of 92.07 billion rupees projected for 1997/98 (April-March).
"One of the options being considered is removing diesel from the administered price mechanism," he said. "This would translate into a price hike of diesel by 25 percent," he added.
The official said the option of removing liquefied petroleum gas and kerosene from administered pricing was ruled out because the rises were too large for poorer citizens to bear. ($1 = 35.7 rupees)
